c0613: Zoning check before signing: restaurant use, Type I hood, gas service and seats
c0616: Ask the city planning (zoning) office whether the zoning allows a restaurant with rotisseries and fryers, whether the space can take a Type I hood with a duct up to the roof, and what occupancy load it allows. Then ask the fire marshal in writing what the hood and fire suppression requirements are. With no exhaust path to the roof, there are no rotisseries or fryers.
c0617: Decide gas or charcoal rotisseries BEFORE signing the lease (charcoal = solid fuel: dedicated exhaust, NFPA 96, listed appliance)
c0619: Gas rotisseries (the plan's case) work with a standard Type I hood and gas service installed by a licensed gas contractor. A charcoal rotisserie, like the oven of a Peruvian pollo a la brasa place, is a solid-fuel appliance under NFPA 96: it needs its own exhaust, a spark arrester and daily ash removal, and the fire marshal will want a listed (UL/ETL) appliance, plus NSF/ANSI 4 certification for the health department. Rotisseries imported from Peru may have no listing, and air quality rules vary: ask your air district. It is a product decision, not a decoration one: ask the fire marshal in writing whether your space can take it.
c0620: Size the rotisseries with your Sunday count (48 birds per load, loads of 75-90 minutes)
c0621: With the "Rotisserie" tab of the kit's calculator: how many chickens you sell on Sunday, how many fit per load and how many loads you can run before the Sunday lunch peak. The plan uses two 8-spit gas rotisseries (48 birds per load each); peak months and holidays run tight. The rotisseries have to fit in the space together with their Type I hood.
c0630: Business license + sales tax permit (state and city)
c0632: Register with your state revenue department for a sales tax permit and with your city or county for a business license. Some states also ask for a separate food seller or retail license. Rules, fees and timing vary by state, so confirm them with your CPA before you open and collect sales tax from your first sale.
c0643: Bring the complete financial plan, with the month-by-month cash flow. Ask for quotes on equipment leasing for the rotisseries, the walk-in cooler and the fryers, and ask each lender about the SBA Microloan (up to $50,000) as a complement. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection (often around 10% for SBA start-ups; many want 20-30%).
c0647: Get quotes for general liability, liquor liability (if you will serve beer and wine), property and workers' comp. Tell the broker you cook on gas with rotisseries and fryers, and ask about equipment breakdown and spoilage coverage for the walk-in cooler.
c0650: Use the dropdown: ✓, ☐, N/A. ✓ = done, ☐ = pending, N/A = not applicable and comes out of the total.
c0653: Choose the space: second-generation restaurant space of about 1,600 sq ft (149 sq m) with a route for the Type I hood up to the roof
c0655: Kitchen and rotisserie area visible from the street, a counter with a heated display, a dining room with 40 seats, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and storage. A residential neighborhood with family foot traffic on weekends and easy parking for pickup orders.
c0659: Refrigeration, exhaust fans, HVAC and the dishwasher on electric service; rotisseries, fryers and range on gas (natural or propane). Two rotisseries of about 177,500 BTU each plus the fryers need a gas service and regulator sized for the load, with a gas permit. Ask the utility for the lead time and the cost.
c0662: Dedicated Type I hood and a continuous, grease-tight duct up to the roof, through a shaft or an exterior wall, with the landlord's written approval if it crosses common areas. Ask your mechanical contractor for the exhaust airflow and the makeup air.
c0664: The plan counts two months of rent before opening and a two-month security deposit. Ask for free rent while the build-out, the hood and the gas work last.
c0665: Lease with restaurant use, hood rights and a beer & wine license contingency
c0668: It should say "restaurant" or "rotisserie chicken restaurant with kitchen", authorize the build-out and the duct to the roof, and let you out of the lease if you cannot get your beer & wine license.
c0672: Kitchen and counter layout, electrical load, occupancy, ventilation, ADA accessibility, the gas installation and the hood and duct route to the roof. Ask your city (and your air district, if there is one) for its fire, mechanical and air quality requirements.
c0675: Zoning approval and the certificate of occupancy come from your city or county, and the rules vary. In your zoning check, ask which approvals your space needs (change of use, building permit, fire marshal sign-off) and in what order.
c0679: Licensed gas contractor, gas permit and inspection for two rotisseries + fryers
c0682: Gas permit, pressure test and final inspection of the lines and appliances, and a regulator and meter sized for the rotisseries, fryers and range. Keep the paperwork: the fire marshal, the health department and your insurer may ask for it. Work by an unlicensed installer will not pass inspection.
c0683: Type I hood, UL 300 suppression and makeup air (charcoal: separate solid-fuel exhaust and spark arrester)
c0686: Over the rotisseries and fryers: Type I hood with grease filters, UL 300 fire suppression system and makeup air, installed to your local fire and mechanical code. With charcoal or wood (solid fuel), NFPA 96 asks for a dedicated exhaust, a spark arrester and daily ash removal; with gas rotisseries, the standard hood is enough. Ask your air district about particulate rules.
c0687: Build-out with smooth, cleanable surfaces in the kitchen and prep areas
c0689: Smooth, cleanable walls, non-slip floors (also around the rotisseries), cleanable ceilings, hands-free handwashing sinks, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and sound insulation if you have neighbors.
c0692: Hot and cold water in the kitchen, floor drains with a grease interceptor (the rotisseries and fryers produce a lot of grease) and HVAC for the dining room.
c0693: Fire marshal sign-off of the hood and suppression system + Class K extinguisher
c0695: Hood with exhaust fan and grease filters covering the whole cooking line, tied to the dedicated duct, with a UL 300 suppression system and a Class K extinguisher. Ask the installer for the airflow, the makeup air and the filter cleaning plan. The fire marshal inspects it before you can cook.
c0696: Electrical final inspection and certificate of occupancy
c0700: Sign permit; rotisseries visible from the street; pre-order phone and website on the sign
c0703: Ask in your zoning check whether your city requires a separate sign permit. Put the pre-order phone number and the website where they can be read from the street.
c0706: Buy listed equipment (UL/ETL, NSF/ANSI 4): two gas rotisseries, heated display, fryers, range
c0707: Two 8-spit gas rotisseries (a Pegasus CR-8G lists at $6,011 retail and holds 48 birds per load; the plan budgets $13,000 for the pair with freight and installation), a heated display that holds 135 °F (57 °C) or above, two fryers and a range. Ask for the technical data sheet, birds per spit, gas consumption, lead time and installation.
c0708: Walk-in, prep table and reach-in freezer
c0710: Walk-in cooler for raw and marinated chicken at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, a reach-in freezer and a refrigerated case that keeps the sides at the counter at 41 °F (5 °C) or below.
c0714: Apply to your local health department for plan review (Food Code 8-201.11) before construction, then for the health permit and the pre-opening inspection. Selling chicken or sauces to other businesses can fall under a different license: ask your health department.
c0715: Raw and marinated chicken at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, on the bottom shelf, date-marked (WOG: no giblets)
c0718: Buy USDA-inspected chicken from an approved source and receive it at 41 °F (5 °C) or below; the marinated raw chicken is held at 41 °F (5 °C) or below as well, below any ready-to-eat food. The plan buys birds WOG (without giblets), so there are no giblets to store. Log the temperature at every delivery.
c0719: Separate raw-chicken prep sink and table, color-coded boards, never wash raw chicken
c0721: Spit and marinate on a stainless-steel table SEPARATE from the one you serve from, with its own boards and utensils. Raw chicken is not washed: it splashes and contaminates the area.
c0722: Get your county's rules for cooking and hot holding chicken in writing and write your rotisserie SOP: probe the thigh at 165 °F (74 °C) and log it
c0723: Each state adopts its own edition of the FDA Food Code and your county may add rules. The Food Code requires poultry to reach 165 °F (74 °C) (3-401.11); the plan's SOP probes the thickest part of the thigh on every load and logs it. Browned outside does not mean done next to the bone.
c0724: Heated display at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, time marked on every load (4-hour limit; TPHC only with a written procedure)
c0726: Hot holding is 135 °F (57 °C) or above (Food Code 3-501.16). The plan's SOP keeps the display hot and marks the time on every load: at 4 hours, or if a bird drops below 135 °F, cool it at once with a log for tomorrow's sandwich or bowl, or throw it out. Never put it back in the display without reheating it to 165 °F (74 °C). Under time as a public health control instead (TPHC, 3-501.19), with the time marked and a written procedure, the chicken is thrown out at 4 hours, never cooled.
c0727: Leftover chicken cooled from 135 °F (57 °C) to 70 °F (21 °C) in 2 hours and to 41 °F (5 °C) within 6 hours, logged; reheat to 165 °F
c0729: What is left at closing is either held at 135 °F (57 °C) or above or cooled from 135 °F to 70 °F in 2 hours and to 41 °F within 6 hours in total (3-501.14). Reuse it the next day in the sandwich or bowl, reheated to 165 °F (74 °C) for hot holding (3-403.11). Log how many birds are left every day.
c0730: Aji verde, huancaina and other sauces: TCS foods at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, date-marked
c0731: Sauces made with mayonnaise, fresh cheese or evaporated milk are TCS (time/temperature control for safety) foods: keep them at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, date-mark them and discard them on time. Cooked rice and beans are TCS foods too (B. cereus): keep them at 135 °F (57 °C) or above. No raw egg in any sauce unless it is pasteurized.
c0732: Label the birds and sides you pack for self-service (3-602.11)
c0733: A whole chicken bagged in the heated display for self-service, or sides packed ahead, need a label with the name of the food, the ingredients with the major allergens, the net quantity, and your business name and address (Food Code 3-602.11; check your state's rules). Food bagged to order and handed over by staff does not need the full label, but still tell the customer about allergens.
c0736: Lot and date of the chicken, receiving temperature, cooler temperatures, probe temperatures, display temperatures, cooling logs for leftovers and the supplier of every ingredient.
c0737: Recipe cards with the 9 major allergens (soy and wheat in the marinade; milk and egg in the sauces)
c0738: Marinade (soy and wheat from the soy sauce, wheat or barley if it has beer), aji verde (egg and milk, depending on the recipe), huancaina (milk, and wheat from the crackers), sandwich bun (wheat; sesame if it has seeds) and fries or yuca fries from a shared fryer (cross-contact). With the kit's calculator, the cost of each one.
c0741: On delivery marketplaces and on your own website, allergens must be visible before the customer orders. Check the listing of each product on each platform.
c0744: Insulated bags and packaging that keep the food hot (135 °F (57 °C) or above) in transit, also for marketplace delivery: a whole chicken travels well, fries do not.
c0749: The federal minimum wage is $7.25/h, but your state or city may be higher: use the highest. The plan assumes at least $15/h for everyone; put your actual lowest hourly rate in the "0. Assumptions" tab of the financial plan.
c0752: Hire the second rotisserie cook before opening (7 days)
c0753: Have them learn with you to spit, load, probe and carve before opening. If only you can run the rotisseries, one sick day closes you on Sunday, your peak day.
c0757: Sunday and peak-day schedule (2 rotisserie cooks + 3 on the counter)
c0759: The shop is open 7 days and Sunday is the peak. Schedule two rotisserie cooks and three people on the counter, plus dish and prep, and treat holidays like a Sunday.
c0764: Check what your state requires: a Certified Food Protection Manager on site (Food Code 2-102.12) and food handler cards for the staff. Train on handwashing, raw and cooked separation, probe temperatures, display and cooling logs, allergens and cross-contact.
c0765: Rotisserie training: spitting, loading, probing at 165 °F (74 °C), carving
c0766: Sizing and trussing the bird, spitting with no gaps, load order, thigh probe and carving into halves and quarters. It is an investment, not an expense.
c0769: Cover the main hazards: burns from the rotisseries, hot spits and fryers, cuts when carving and spitting, gas, heat and lifting. OSHA expects a written safety plan and training.
c0775: Allergen notice at the counter and online
c0776: Each marinade, sauce and side with its allergens in plain view of the customer: soy and wheat in the marinade, egg in the aji verde and milk in the huancaina, depending on your recipe. Review it whenever a recipe changes.
c0777: Never promise "gluten-free" with a shared fryer (21 CFR 101.91)
c0779: Under the FDA rule (21 CFR 101.91), "gluten-free" means less than 20 ppm of gluten as served. The marinade has soy sauce and beer (wheat, barley), and yuca fries or fries cooked in the same fryer as breaded items break the promise. Disclose the allergens and the cross-contact; do not promise it.
c0782: Choose your style (Peruvian pollo a la brasa in the case) and your menu
c0784: A weekend take-out rotisserie, a neighborhood counter-service rotisserie chicken restaurant (this plan), peri-peri chicken or charcoal Peruvian chicken: each with a different investment, space and margin. Food trucks have their own plan: the Food Truck Business Plan Kit.
c0785: Short menu (quarter, half, whole, family meal, sandwich/bowl) costed with the calculator
c0786: Cost the quarter, half and whole chicken and every combo (with yuca fries, with rice & beans, the Sunday family meal): the chicken alone leaves little, the margin is in what goes with it. Use the kit's Rotisserie Chicken Yield & Costing Calculator.
c0787: Sales tax on the menu: one rate; check your state's to-go rules
c0789: The plan uses a single sales tax rate (8% as an example). Some states tax to-go food differently from dine-in, so check your state and city rates with your CPA and set them up in the POS and on every delivery marketplace.
c0793: Some cities and states ban or charge for single-use plastic bags, foam containers and utensils. Check your city's rules before you order family-meal boxes, vented clamshells, foil bags and sauce cups.
c0794: Two USDA-inspected chicken suppliers (fixed 3.0 lb (1.4 kg) WOG birds, received at 41 °F (5 °C) or below)
c0795: Birds of a fixed size, 3.0 lb (1.4 kg) WOG, received at 41 °F (5 °C) or below and logged. The price of chicken moves during the year: two suppliers and the price in writing. An uneven size throws off your loads and your costing.
c0796: Frozen yuca and fries, oil, packaging, sodas and a beer & wine distributor
c0797: Frozen or fresh yuca and potatoes (fresh lowers the cost but needs peeling and cutting), high-oleic frying oil, family-meal boxes, vented clamshells and sauce cups. The plan estimates them with reference prices: put your own.
c0798: Used cooking oil pickup and drip-tray grease
c0799: Contract with a licensed waste / grease hauler to pick up the oil from the fryers and the grease from the rotisserie drip trays, with a receipt for every pickup. Never down the drain.
c0800: Pre-order system: phone, online ordering, pickup slots and deposits for party trays
c0801: Pre-orders with name, phone number and pickup time, closed on Saturday for Sunday: that tells you how many birds to load. A sign at the counter and the phone number on the bags.
c0803: Read the commission (it changes with the marketplace, the plan tier and the zone), how often they pay out, who funds the promotions and what the tablet costs. Set a ceiling for marketplace sales and track it every month. Pickup at the counter pays no commission: push it with price.
c0807: Brand, photos and website with menu, allergens and pre-orders
c0810: Real photos of the rotisseries and the combos; a website with the menu, allergens, hours, the pre-order phone number and a privacy policy for each channel.
c0811: Google Business Profile, Yelp, Instagram + music licensing (ASCAP/BMI/SESAC)
c0812: Opening hours, photos of the rotisseries and a reply to every review. If you play music, you need performing-rights licenses (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC).
c0819: Cleaning plan for kitchen, rotisseries and display
c0820: Rotisseries, spits and drip tray, fryers, hood filters, heated display, raw-chicken table and refrigeration, with a log.
c0821: Test loads with the full menu (time each load)
c0823: Several test loads to tune the marinade, the cooking time, the probe and the carving, and a rehearsal Sunday with pre-orders from friends before you open.
c0826: Walk-in, thigh probe on every load, heated display, cooling of leftovers, sauces and the cleaning sheet; fix any deviation before you serve.
c0829: Allergen cards, labels on packaged food, traceability, temperature, cooling and cleaning logs, training records and pest control.
c0833: NFPA 96 sets the frequency by cooking volume and fuel: the plan budgets quarterly cleanings by a certified company because of the rotisserie grease (solid fuel such as charcoal means monthly). Keep every cleaning report, and clean the grease filters as your cleaning plan says.
c0834: Fire suppression inspection every 6 months and annual rotisserie and gas service
c0836: The fire suppression system is inspected every 6 months, and the burners, motor and spits of the rotisseries get a service once a year, with the gas lines checked by your licensed gas contractor. Write down the dates.
c0837: Measure cooked yield and load time and recalculate (calculator)
c0839: Weigh five raw and cooked chickens from the same load, time a full load and note the birds left at closing; take the averages to the calculator. The cooked yield and the load time in the plan are Kit estimates.
c0840: Holiday pre-order plan: Mother's Day, Super Bowl Sunday, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve (pickup slots, deposits, order cap = rotisserie capacity, whole crew)
c0842: Mother's Day, Super Bowl Sunday, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve are pre-order peaks, and May, July and December are the plan's busiest months. Prepare the schedule, the loads and the chicken order early.
c0845: Sales, commission, promotions and packaging: if marketplace sales grow, or their margin does not cover the commission, cut back or raise prices. Own delivery only with W-2 drivers and when the volume pays for it.
c0847: Covers per day, average check, birds sold, cost of goods and labor against the P&L in the Excel; review your costing whenever the price of chicken changes.
